en: Thus have I heard: the Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovādasutta, the sixty-first discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Rāhula was dwelling at Ambalaṭṭhikā.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to Ambalaṭṭhikā, where the Venerable Rāhula was staying.
The Venerable Rāhula saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he prepared a seat and water for washing the feet.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, he washed his feet.
The Venerable Rāhula, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One, having set aside a small amount of water remaining in the water-vessel, addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Rāhula, do you see this small amount of water remaining set aside in the water-vessel?
“I do, Bhante.
“In just such a small measure, Rāhula, is the asceticism of those who feel no shame in telling a deliberate lie.”
Then the Blessed One, having discarded the small remainder of water, addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Do you see, Rāhula, that small remainder of water which has been discarded?
“I do, Bhante.”
“Rāhula, the ascetic life of those who have no shame in telling deliberate lies is thus cast away.
Then the Blessed One turned that water vessel upside down and addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Do you see, Rāhula, this water vessel turned upside down?”
“Yes, Bhante.
“Thus, Rāhula, the asceticism of those who have no shame in telling a deliberate lie is overturned.
Then the Blessed One turned that water-pot upright and addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Rāhula, do you see this water-vessel as empty and void?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Rāhula, the asceticism of those who have no sense of shame regarding deliberate lying is empty and void.”
"Just as, Rāhula, a king’s elephant— possessing tusks like chariot poles, well-born, noble, and accustomed to battle—
when engaged in combat, performs its work with its forefeet, performs its work with its hindfeet, performs its work with its forequarters,
performs its work with its hindquarters, performs its work with its head, and even with its ears."
It performs work with its forefeet, it performs work with its tusks, and it performs work with its tail; yet it protects its trunk.
Then the elephant-rider thinks:
"This is indeed the king’s elephant—possessing tusks like chariot-poles, well-bred, noble, a veteran of battle—who, having entered the fray, [performs these feats] with its forefeet..."
He performs his work with his forefeet, he performs his work with his hind feet... [and so on] ...he even performs his work with his tail;
yet he guards his trunk.
The life of the king’s elephant is not yet abandoned.”
But when, Rāhula, a king’s elephant— possessed of tusks as long as chariot poles, well-born, of noble breed, and experienced in battle—
enters the fray and performs its work with its forefeet, its hind feet, ...pe... its tail, and its trunk, then the elephant-rider thinks thus:
“This royal elephant, indeed, has tusks as long as chariot poles, is powerful, well-bred, and experienced in battle;
when engaged in combat, it performs its task with its forefeet, it performs its task with its hindfeet, it performs its task with its forequarters,
it performs its task with its hindquarters, it performs its task with its head, and it performs its task with its ears.”
"He performs his work with his tusks, he performs his work with his tail, and he performs his work with his trunk.
The life of the king’s elephant is indeed surrendered;
there is now nothing that the king’s elephant will not do."
"In the same way, Rāhula, for anyone who has no sense of shame regarding intentional lying, I say there is no evil they would not do.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: 'I will not speak a falsehood even as a joke.'"
“What do you think, Rāhula,
what is the purpose of a mirror?
“It is for the purpose of reflection, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Rāhula, action should be performed with the body after repeated reflection;
action should be performed with speech after repeated reflection; action should be performed with the mind after repeated reflection.
Whatever bodily action you wish to perform, Rāhula, that very bodily action must be reflected upon:”
‘Suppose I desire to perform this bodily action; would this bodily action of mine lead to my own affliction, or lead to the affliction of others, or lead to the affliction of both?
This bodily action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
If, Rāhula, upon reflection you should know thus:

“Rāhula, if upon reflection you should know: ‘This bodily action that I wish to perform might lead to my own affliction, or it might lead to the affliction of others, or it might lead to the affliction of both;
this bodily action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result,’ then, Rāhula, such a bodily action should not be performed even with effort.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:”
‘Whatever bodily action I wish to do, if that bodily action would lead neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both— this bodily action is wholesome,
having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result,’ such, Rāhula, is the kind of bodily action you should perform.
While performing that bodily action, Rāhula, you should reflect upon that very same bodily action:
‘What if I were to examine this bodily action that I am performing: does this bodily action of mine lead to my own affliction, or to the affliction of others, or to the affliction of both?
This bodily action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result’?
And if, Rāhula, upon examining it, you should know thus:
“Rāhula, if upon reflection you should know: ‘This bodily action that I am performing leads to my own affliction, leads to the affliction of others, and leads to the affliction of both;
this bodily action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result,’ then you should withdraw such a bodily action, Rāhula.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:”
“Rāhula, when you think: ‘This bodily action that I am performing does not lead to my own affliction, nor does it lead to the affliction of others, nor does it lead to the affliction of both;
this bodily action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result,’ then, Rāhula, you may undertake such a bodily action.
Even after you have performed that bodily action, Rāhula, you must reflect upon that very same bodily action:”

‘What if I have performed this bodily action; this bodily action of mine leads to my own affliction, leads to the affliction of others, and leads to the affliction of both—it is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?
If, Rāhula, upon reflection you should know thus:
‘Whatever bodily action I have performed here, this bodily action of mine leads to my own affliction, leads to the affliction of others, and leads to the affliction of both;

this bodily action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result’—such bodily action, Rāhula, should be confessed by you before the Teacher or before wise companions in the holy life;
it should be revealed and made plain. Having confessed it, revealed it, and made it plain, you should undertake restraint for the future.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
"This bodily action that I have performed does not lead to my own affliction, nor does it lead to the affliction of others, nor does it lead to the affliction of both;
this bodily action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result," then, Rāhula, you should dwell with joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
“Rāhula, whatever verbal action you wish to perform, that very verbal action must be reflected upon:
‘If I were to perform this verbal action, would it lead to my own affliction, or to the affliction of others, or to the affliction of both?
Is this verbal action unwholesome, with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?’”
If, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
"This verbal action which I wish to perform would lead to my own affliction, or it would lead to the affliction of others, or it would lead to the affliction of both;
this verbal action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result"—then, Rāhula, such a verbal action should not be performed by you even with effort.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
"This verbal action which I wish to perform would lead neither to my own affliction nor to the affliction of others;
this verbal action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result"—then, Rāhula, such a verbal action should be performed by you.
Rāhula, while performing an action by way of speech, you should reflect upon that very verbal action:
“Is this action I am performing by way of speech leading to my own affliction, leading to the affliction of others, or leading to the affliction of both?
Is this verbal action unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?”
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
"This verbal action that I am performing leads to my own affliction, leads to the affliction of others, and leads to the affliction of both;
this verbal action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result," then you should withdraw such verbal action, Rāhula.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
“This verbal action that I am performing does not lead to my own affliction, nor does it lead to the affliction of others, nor does it lead to the affliction of both;
this verbal action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result,” then, Rāhula, you may undertake such verbal action.
Rāhula, even after you have performed an action with speech, that very same verbal action must be reflected upon thus:
"Did I perform this action with speech that leads to my own affliction, leads to the affliction of others, and leads to the affliction of both?
Is this verbal action unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?"
If, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
“This verbal action that I have performed leads to my own affliction, leads to the affliction of others, and leads to the affliction of both;

this verbal action is unwholesome, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result,” then, Rāhula, such a verbal action must be confessed by you to the Teacher or to wise fellow-celibates; it must be revealed and made manifest.
Having taught, revealed, and made plain [this], one should undertake restraint for the future.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:

"This verbal action that I have performed does not lead to my own affliction, nor does it lead to the affliction of others, nor does it lead to the affliction of both; ... [then you should continue to engage in such speech]."
‘This verbal action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result. With that very joy and gladness, Rāhula, you should dwell training day and night in wholesome states.
Whatever mental action you wish to perform, Rāhula, that very mental action should be reflected upon by you:
‘If I wish to perform this mental action, would this mental action of mine lead to my own affliction, or lead to the affliction of others, or lead to the affliction of both?’”
‘This unwholesome mental action has suffering as its outcome, suffering as its result’?
If, Rāhula, upon reflection you should know thus:
‘This mental action that I wish to perform would lead to my own affliction, or it would lead to the affliction of others, or it would lead to the affliction of both,’ [then you should refrain].”
‘This unwholesome mental action has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result,’ then, Rāhula, such a mental action should not be performed by you even with effort.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know:
‘This mental action that I wish to perform would lead neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both—’
‘This mental action is wholesome; it has happiness as its outcome, happiness as its result,’ such, Rāhula, is the kind of mental action you should perform.
While performing that mental action, Rāhula, you should review that very mental action:

‘Does this mental action that I am performing lead to my own affliction, or to the affliction of others, or to the affliction of both? Is it unwholesome, with suffering as its outcome, suffering as its result?’”
‘This unwholesome mental action has suffering as its outcome, suffering as its result’?
But if, Rāhula, upon reflection you should know thus:
‘This mental action that I am performing with the mind leads to my own affliction, it leads to the affliction of others, and it leads to the affliction of both;’
‘This unwholesome mental action has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result,’ then you should withdraw such a mental action, Rāhula.
But if, upon reflection, you should know:
‘This mental action that I am performing with the mind leads neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both—’
‘This mental action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result,’ then you should undertake such mental action, Rāhula.
But even after you have performed that mental action with the mind, Rāhula, you should reflect upon that very mental action:
‘Did I indeed perform this mental action? Does this mental action of mine lead to my own affliction, or to the affliction of others, or to the affliction of both?’”
‘This unwholesome mental action has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result’?
If, Rāhula, upon reflection you should know thus:
‘This mental action that I have performed with the mind leads to my own affliction, it leads to the affliction of others, and it leads to the affliction of both—’
‘This unwholesome mental action has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result,’ then, Rāhula, you should feel dread, shame, and disgust toward such a mental action;
having felt dread, shame, and disgust, you should undertake restraint for the future.
But if, Rāhula, while reflecting, you should know thus:
‘Whatever mental action I have performed here, this mental action of mine leads neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both;
this mental action is wholesome, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result’—with that very joy and gladness, Rāhula, you should dwell, training day and night in wholesome states.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, Rāhula, in the past purified their bodily action... [and so on].

They purified their verbal action; they purified their mental action. All of them, having repeatedly reflected in this very way, purified their bodily action; having repeatedly reflected, they purified their verbal action;
having repeatedly reflected, they purified their mental action.
"Rāhula, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will purify their bodily action,
will purify their verbal action, and will purify their mental action— all of them will do so by repeatedly reflecting upon it;
they will purify their bodily action by repeatedly reflecting upon it, and they will purify their verbal action by repeatedly reflecting upon it."
“They will purify it; by repeatedly reflecting, they will purify mental action.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, Rāhula, at present purify bodily action, purify verbal action, and purify mental action, all of them do so precisely in this way, by repeatedly reflecting.

They purify bodily action; they purify verbal action by repeatedly reflecting; they purify mental action by repeatedly reflecting. Therefore, Rāhula, "I shall purify bodily action by repeatedly reflecting," [you should train yourself]. Paccavekkhitvā... [you should train yourself]. Paccavekkhitvā... [you should train yourself]. “Having reflected, I will purify my verbal action; having reflected again and again, I will purify my mental action.
It is in this way, Rāhula, that you should train yourself.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Rāhula was uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovāda Sutta is finished; it is the first.
